findings.question: Which feeder supplies Load R11, and through which lines does its power come from the external grid?
findings.answer:
Load R11 is at **Bus 11**. The external grid connects through **Transformer T0 (Bus 0–Bus 1)**, then **Line L0 (Bus 1–Bus 2)** and **Line L1 (Bus 2–Bus 3)**.

From Bus 3, the network is meshed, so there isn’t one unique feeder route to Bus 11. Topological routes include:

- **L2 (Bus 3–Bus 4) → L13 (Bus 4–Bus 11)**
- **L9 (Bus 3–Bus 8) → L6 (Bus 8–Bus 9) → L7 (Bus 9–Bus 10) → L8 (Bus 10–Bus 11)**

These are connected paths, not a measurement of how power is split between them at a particular time.

findings.question: Why would losing the line Bus_28 -> Bus_29 be critical at 18:00 on 6 January when it was not at 15:00?
findings.answer:
With **Bus_28 → Bus_29 [L38] out at both times**, Bus_29 was only just within the voltage limit at 15:00: **0.952 p.u.** against a **0.950 p.u.** minimum. By 18:00 it had fallen to **0.931 p.u.**, a **0.021 p.u.** drop that put it below the limit.

The difference is mainly higher demand near Bus_29. Demand at Bus_28 and Bus_29 rose from **10.50 MW to 12.77 MW**; that local increase accounts for **78.4%** of the voltage fall, with Bus_29’s demand responsible for most of the local effect. Higher demand elsewhere accounts for the remaining **21.6%**. Changes in the five units’ output were ruled out as a meaningful contributor.

So the line outage is the same in both cases; at 15:00 the system had only about **0.002 p.u.** of voltage margin at Bus_29 after the outage, and the later demand increase pushed it below the limit. Demand reactive power was derived using the default **0.95 lagging power factor**.

findings.question: Build a new 0.4 kV substation at Bus 9 with two 0.63 MVA transformers (vk 6 %, vkr 1 %) and connect a 0.8 MW data centre to it. Is it N-1 secure?
findings.answer:
On proposal **dc_bus9_04kv** (the base network plus the new 0.4 kV substation at Bus 9, two 0.63 MVA transformers, and a 0.8 MW data-centre load), **the modeled system is not N-1 secure**. This is a what-if proposal; it does not modify the base network.

- **At 18:00**, the N-1 screen found violations for **12 of 18 outages**. The worst reported undervoltage was **0.914 p.u.** at the new data-centre bus following loss of **Line 7-8**. The screen also found outages that disconnected load.
- In the **hourly scan of Jan 1**, the proposal had voltage violations in **17 of 24 sampled hours**; its lowest voltage was **0.920 p.u.** at the new bus at **18:00**. The base had no violations in those hourly samples.
- **Transformer-model caveat:** the two transformers are represented together as one branch, so the N-1 screen removes both together; it does **not** separately test loss of just one transformer. Also, at the proposal’s assumed data-centre power factor of 0.95, 0.8 MW is about **0.84 MVA**, above the **0.63 MVA** rating of one transformer. The proposal therefore does not establish that the centre could be supplied after one unit is lost.

The screen at 00:00 had no voltage or thermal violations, but did identify load-disconnecting outages. Screens were run at different timestamps; the results above are labeled by their respective times. The data-centre load was assumed flat at pf 0.95; measured loads used pf 0.97.

- Important modelling limitation: the two 0.63 MVA transformers are represented as **one branch**, so the outage removes both together. The study therefore does not simulate the loss of just one transformer with the other remaining. Also, at the stated 0.95 lagging power factor, 0.8 MW corresponds to about **0.84 MVA**, above the 0.63 MVA rating of one unit; a single remaining unit would be undersized by nameplate.
- The base network also fails the N‑1 criterion in this study because contingencies disconnect existing loads.

The proposal uses a flat 0.8 MW data-centre load at assumed pf 0.95 lagging; transformer no-load losses and magnetising current were set to zero. To assess single-transformer redundancy faithfully, the two transformers need to be represented as separate outage elements.

findings.answer:
On proposal *inj_setpoint* (Gen_bus12 voltage set-point changed from 1.025 to 0.950 p.u.), Bus_29 violates its lower voltage limit at **18:00 on 6 January**, while it is only just above the limit on the base.

The comparison points to the set-point change as the immediate reason: **Bus_29 falls from 0.954 p.u. on the base to 0.942 p.u. on the proposal** (limit: 0.950 p.u.). Because Gen_bus12 is voltage-controlled, the proposal holds Bus_12 at 0.950 p.u.; its reactive output shifts from **+11.82 MVAr** on the base to **−11.40 MVAr** on the proposal. That reduced local voltage support coincides with a broader voltage drop: for example, Bus_28 falls from 0.969 to 0.957 p.u. Bus_29 is a 135 kV bus with a 5.58 MW load, connected to Bus_26 and Bus_28 by lines L37 and L38, so the drop reaches it through that part of the network.

The base Bus_29 had only **0.004 p.u.** of margin, so it was already close to the limit. Line loadings remain below 100% in both cases; this is a voltage-limit issue, not a thermal overload. I can show the direct comparison, but I don’t have a causal-attribution tool here to quantify each factor’s share.

The lowest reading was **0.944 p.u. at 19:30**, or **0.006 p.u. below the limit**. There were six below-limit readings in the 17:00–23:45 window.

findings.question: Build a new 0.4 kV substation at Bus 9 with two 0.63 MVA transformers (vk 6 %, vkr 1 %) and connect a 0.8 MW data centre to it. Is it N-1 secure?
findings.answer:
On proposal **dc_bus9_04kv** (a 0.4 kV bus at Bus 9, two 0.63 MVA transformers, and a flat 0.8 MW data-centre load), **it is not N-1 secure** at the study point, 2000-01-01 00:00.

The N-1 sweep reports the data-centre bus disconnected when its transformer branch is lost, cutting off the full 0.8 MW load. There were no voltage or thermal violations reported, but that does **not** mean the case is secure: the load was disconnected. The model represents the two parallel transformers as one branch, so its outage removes both together rather than testing the loss of just one.

The **Most headroom** option leaves L30 with the most reported clearance: **31.7 percentage points below rating**. It moves all five generators’ active power and voltage set-points. The least-import option also meets the requested ceiling, but L30 sits right at the 75% limit.

All five options passed their AC power-flow checks with no violations. findings.finding: 2.5 — “exceeded its 100% limit for 10 quarter-hour intervals (2.5 hours in total), including a sustained episode from”  (nearest source 2.25 at investigate.events[1].hours_outside)
findings.question: Why was the line from the external grid outside its limit for longer on 6 January than on 5 January?
findings.answer:
The overloaded external-grid branch was **Bus_0 → Bus_1 [L0]**; the other external-grid branch, **Bus_0 → Bus_2 [L1]**, had no overloads on either day.

On Jan 6, L0 exceeded its 100% limit for **10 quarter-hour intervals (2.5 hours in total)**, including a sustained episode from **19:15 to 21:00** that peaked at **134.1%**. On Jan 5 it exceeded the limit for **5 intervals (1.25 hours total)**, peaking at **107.6%**.

The investigations point to **demand as the main driver on both days**. For the sustained Jan 6 episode, demand near L0 accounted for 59.5% of the change and demand elsewhere for another 24.4%. Generation changes contributed in that episode, but they do not consistently explain the longer duration: their effect varied across Jan 5’s episodes. So the evidence points to a stronger, more sustained demand-driven stress on Jan 6—not to a consistent generation-output shift.

📋 Data source: measurements

findings.question: Why was the line from the external grid outside its limit for longer on 6 January than on 5 January?
findings.answer:
The line from the external grid, **Bus_0–Bus_1 [L0]**, was overloaded for **2.5 hours on 6 January**, compared with **1.25 hours on 5 January**. The difference was mainly a demand-driven evening overload: on 6 January, the longest episode ran from **19:15 to 21:00** and peaked at **134.1%** loading. On 5 January, the overloads were shorter, with a peak of **107.6%**.

Demand was identified as the main cause in all three episodes on both days. findings.question: Why was the line from the external grid outside its limit for longer on 6 January than on 5 January?
findings.answer:
The line from the external grid, **Bus_0–Bus_1 [L0]**, was overloaded for **2.5 hours on 6 January**, compared with **1.25 hours on 5 January**. The difference was mainly a demand-driven evening overload: on 6 January, the longest episode ran from **19:15 to 21:00** and peaked at **134.1%** loading. On 5 January, the overloads were shorter, with a peak of **107.6%**.

Demand was identified as the main cause in all three episodes on both days. In the 6 January episodes, demand near the line contributed **59.5–84.5%** of the change into overload, with demand elsewhere contributing **24.4–34.6%**. The unit-output contribution varied; it was not the main explanation for the longer duration.

These percentages describe contributions to the change at each episode’s onset, not a direct comparison of total demand between the two dates. Reactive demand was estimated using the default **0.95 power factor**.

findings.question: Build a new 0.4 kV substation at Bus 9 with two 0.63 MVA transformers (vk 6 %, vkr 1 %) and connect a 0.8 MW data centre to it. Is it N-1 secure?
findings.answer:
On proposal **bus9_datacentre** (base network plus the new 0.4 kV substation and 0.8 MW flat-profile data centre), the network is **not N-1 secure at 2000-01-01 00:00**.

The sweep tested 18 outages. No overload or voltage violations were reported, but **15 outages disconnected load**—so zero listed violations does not mean the system stayed supplied. In particular, loss of the new substation’s transformer branch disconnects the data centre’s **0.80 MW**.

**Important model limitation:** the two 0.63 MVA transformers are represented as one parallel branch, so the sweep takes both out together; it does not test the loss of just one transformer. With the assumed data-centre power factor of 0.95, its apparent demand is about **0.84 MVA**, above one 0.63 MVA unit’s rating, so the specified pair would also need review for single-transformer-out operation. The transformer model assumes zero no-load losses and magnetising current.

📋 Data source: measurements (at the simulation clock; the data-centre load is flat).
